step.text:
The base layer only applies `user-select: none` without the `-webkit-` prefix, while Tailwind utilities include both versions. In Chromium and WebKit browsers, `-webkit-user-select` isn't just an alias—it's a separate property that Blink recognizes, so if a UA stylesheet or another rule sets it, there could be conflicts.

Looking at the compiled CSS more carefully: both my base rule and Tailwind's preflight are in the `@layer base`, and searching through the preflight section shows `user-select` only appears in the utilities and my custom rule, not in the base layer itself. So the CSS should be correct—`body` has `user-select: none` in the base layer and descendants should inherit it.

But the thread bar is still highlighting, which means something's overriding it. Maybe the app is rendering outside the `body` element, or there's a shadow root involved?

Actually, wait—let me reconsider the CSS injection. When Vite HMR pushes the updated stylesheet as a `<style>` tag, the layer order is declared at the top of the file, so the cascade should be preserved. And I've verified that both `selectAll()` via the Edit menu and `⌘A` produce the same behavior in my test as in the app—only content gets selected, not the thread bar.

So the CSS is correct and Chromium's behavior matches my probe. The issue must be something else about how the selection is being created or what's actually getting selected. So when the selection spans from the markdown text across to the chrome elements, Blink doesn't paint the highlight on the `user-select: none` parts — which my probe confirmed. But in the actual app, those chrome elements are getting highlighted, which means they must have a different computed `user-select` value than `none`. Something in the app is overriding it.

Since it's not in the main styles, it has to be coming from an inline style or another stylesheet like tldraw.css or BlockNote's CSS. I should search through the node_modules CSS files to find where `user-select` is being set globally.

Actually, wait — I'm overcomplicating this. The content is inside `body`, so if my rule is on `body`, it should apply. Let me try a different approach: I can either attach to the running Electron renderer with remote debugging to see what's actually happening, or I can grep through the stylesheets the renderer imports to find where `user-select` is being set.

+ ## Scribe
+ 
+ Hold a key, talk, and what you said is written into whatever you were typing in, anywhere on the machine. It is the same whisper Voice already runs, so there is no second model and no service behind it. Where Voice is a way into a thread, this never touches the crew at all: nothing is written down, nothing goes over the wire, and the settings live in `localStorage` the way a terminal is this machine's shell and not the crew's.
+ 
+ - The key is the whole feature and it is the one kind of key electron cannot register, because `globalShortcut` needs a real key in the combination and a bare modifier is not one. `scribe-keys.ts` listens under the window through libuiohook, bound over N-API the way node-pty is, so the binary loads in electron without ever being rebuilt for it. It is loaded through `createRequire` when it is first wanted rather than at the top of the file: a native module that will not load throws on the import, and an app that cannot start because dictation is unavailable is worse than dictation being unavailable.
+ - **Fn cannot be had, on any Mac, by any app.** macOS keeps it below the tap every app reads and it is not in the public hot key API, and libuiohook has no keycode for it either: `input_hook.c` reads four masks on `flagsChanged` and Fn is not among them. Right Option is the default instead, because it is on the built-in keyboard and Right Control is not. Never put Fn back in the list without a native addon of our own to back it.
+ - Four rules make a bare modifier bearable, and they are numbers in `scribeLatch.ts` rather than anything that owns a keyboard, the way the games hold their rules. It does not arm until it has been held alone, so reaching for a shortcut never raises the pill. Any other key pressed while it is down drops the take and lets the shortcut through, which is the whole of what makes plain Control safe to dictate on. A tap latches, so a hold is a hold and a tap is hands free, one rule rather than a mode to pick. And a press while it is latched is what ends it. A tap too quick to have armed still latches, or the key only works for people who are slow about it.
+ - There is a second way in that never goes through the hook, `Control+Command+Space` and `Control+Alt+Space`, registered permanently beside it. The Windows hook is known to go quiet after `getUserMedia` runs in a focused window, which is exactly what this does, so there is always a key that works and the settings page says outright when the good one is not being heard.
+ - The pill is a window of its own at `#scribe`, warmed at boot the way the tray panel is, and for a bigger reason: it holds whisper, and a model fetched at the moment somebody starts talking is a first dictation that arrives a minute late. It never takes focus. `showInactive`, `type: 'panel'` on macOS and `focusable: false` everywhere else, or the caret leaves the app the words were going to. `#root` wears `bare` there, since the glass is the whole of it and a surface behind that glass would be Crew's own color rather than the color of what is really back there.
+ - A long dictation is read while it is still being said. `take.ts` watches for the pauses and hands a finished stretch to whisper as somebody carries on talking, so by the time the key is let go only the tail is left. Every piece carries where it began, and the chunks come back shifted onto the take's own clock, because the gaps between them are half of what the marks are placed from.
+ - Nothing spoken is ever a mark. `tidy` in `scribeTidy.ts` places them from whisper's own punctuation and from the gaps, so "the period after the war" is a sentence about a war. It also drops the fillers, collapses a word said twice, and cuts a correction back: one standing at the head of a sentence takes the whole sentence in front of it, which is how people really dictate. One sentence back and never two.
+ - A bare "hold on" is not a correction. "Hold on, let me check" is somebody asking for a moment, and taking the line before it away is the one mistake here nobody can see happening. "Actually hold on" is a retraction and is in the list.
+ - The reading runs on `device: 'webgpu'` where there is a card and falls back to `wasm` where there is not, which Voice gets for free. + - A failure keeps the sound. Nothing said twice, so trying again costs one press, and what goes to the worker is a copy rather than the buffer itself, since handing a buffer over empties the one here.

+       code: host.code,
+       repoPath: host.repoPath,
+       providers: [makeFakeProvider({ FAKE_CLI_DELAY_MS: String(delayMs) })],
+       reconnectDelayMs: 100
+     })
+     runners.push(runner)
+     runner.connect(host.url)
+     await new Promise<void>(resolve => {
+       runner.onStatus = status => {
+         if (status === 'online') resolve()
+       }
+     })
+   }
+ 
+   const post = (path: string, body: unknown): Promise<{ status: number; body: any }> =>
+     fetch(`${base}${path}`, {
+       method: 'POST',
+       headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
+       body: JSON.stringify(body)
+     }).then(async res => ({ status: res.status, body: await res.json() }))
+ 
+   async function openBoard(delayMs = 1500): Promise<{ ui: TestUi; run: Start }> {
+     const ui = await TestUi.connect(host.url, 'sam', host.code)
+     uis.push(ui)
+     await connectRunner(delayMs)
+     await ui.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'agent.online' && e.agentId === fake)
+     ui.chat('break this down and keep the board', [fake], undefined, ['tickets'])
+     await ui.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'thread.started')
+     return { ui, run: (await ui.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'agent.start')) as Start }
+   }
+

+     const { ui, run } = await openBoard()
+ 
+     const put = await post('/tickets', {

+       tickets: ['Read how the sync loop commits', 'Segment the chat log', 'Cover it with a test']
+     })
+     expect(put.status).toBe(200)
+     expect(put.body.ids).toEqual(['1', '2', '3'])
+ 
+     const first = (await ui.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'ticket.added')) as Added
+     expect(first.threadId).toBe(run.threadId)
+     expect(first.title).toBe('Read how the sync loop commits')
+ 
+     // A title already up is passed over, and the ids carry on from what the
+     // thread holds rather than starting again.
+     const again = await post('/tickets', {
+       promptId: run.promptId,
+       tickets: ['segment the chat log', 'Push it']
+     })
+     expect(again.body.ids).toEqual(['4'])
+ 
+     expect((await post(`/tickets/2`, { promptId: run.promptId, column: 'doing' })).body).toEqual({ ok: true })
+     const moved = (await ui.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'ticket.moved')) as Moved
+     expect(moved.ticketId).toBe('2')
+     expect(moved.column).toBe('doing')
+ 
+     await post(`/tickets/2`, {
+       promptId: run.promptId,
+       column: 'review',
+       note: 'The log seals a segment at a megabyte'
+     })
+     await ui.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'ticket.moved' && e.column === 'review')
+ 
+     expect((await post(`/tickets/2/decision`, { promptId: run.promptId, text: 'Kept the local copy' })).status).toBe(200)
+     const decided = (await ui.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'ticket.decided')) as Decided
+     expect(decided.text).toBe('Kept the local copy')
+ 
+     const asked = await post('/tickets/question', {
+       promptId: run.promptId,
+       ask: 'Key the cache on the commit or on the path?',
+       assumed: 'the commit',
+       options: ['the commit', 'the path']
+     })
+     expect(asked.body).toEqual({ ok: true })
+     const question = (await ui.waitForEvent(e => e.kind === 'ticket.asked')) as Asked
+     expect(question.askId).toBeTruthy()
+     expect(question.options).toEqual(['the commit', 'the path'])
+ 
+     const board = boardOf([], ui.events.filter(e => isTicketEvent(e.kind)) as TicketEvent[])
+     expect(board.tickets.map(ticket => ticket.title)).toEqual([
+       'Read how the sync loop commits',
+       'Segment the chat log',
+       'Cover it with a test',
+       'Push it'
+     ])
+     expect(board.tickets[1].column).toBe('review')
+     expect(board.tickets[1].review).toBe('The log seals a segment at a megabyte')
+     expect(board.tickets[1].decisions).toEqual(['Kept the local copy'])
+     expect(board.questions[0].ask).toBe('Key the cache on the commit or on the path?')
+   })
+

Scribe is built and in. Here is what landed and what I need from you.

## It works on real speech

`yarn scribe-check` runs the real model over real speech and puts it through the real tidying:

```
said:    So um I think we should we should ship it today. Actually, wait. Let us ship it tomorrow.
written: Let us ship it tomorrow.
```

Filler gone, the stutter collapsed, and the correction reached back and took the whole sentence in front of it.

## What is there

**The key.** Right Option on Mac, Right Ctrl on Windows, through libuiohook. It does not arm until held alone, so reaching for ⌘C never raises the pill; any other key drops the take and lets the shortcut through; a tap latches and the next press ends it. `Control+Command+Space` is registered permanently alongside, because the Windows hook is known to go quiet after a microphone opens and I would not gamble the feature on it.

**The pill.** Its own window at `#scribe`, warmed at boot, never takes focus. Glass, an X in a `bg-fg/10` circle, the bars across the middle, the white check on the right. Reading turns the check into a spinner. A failure says so and keeps the sound, so trying again is one press.

**Speed.** WebGPU with two fallbacks, and Voice gets it free. A long dictation is read in pieces while you are still talking, so on release only the tail is left.

**Punctuation is automatic and never spoken**, as you asked. "The period after the war" stays a sentence about a war.

Settings are a tab under You. Nothing about Scribe is written down, sent, or shown to the crew.

## Three calls I made against the plan

**Fn is impossible.** Not hard, impossible. macOS keeps it below the event tap every app reads, and I read libuiohook's source to confirm it has no keycode for it either. Right Option is the default and the settings page says why in one line. Getting Fn needs a native addon of our own.

**I dropped Silero.** It pulls a second complete onnxruntime alongside the one transformers.js already ships. For push-to-talk the key already brackets the utterance, so all it buys is trimming the silence off both ends, which `trim.ts` now does off the signal we already have. Bad trade for the risk. Say the word and I will add it.

**A bare "hold on" is not a correction.** Scope flagged it and was right: "Hold on, let me check" retracts nothing, and eating the line before it is the one mistake nobody can see happen. "Actually hold on" is in the list.

## What you need to do

On first use macOS will ask for Accessibility, which the key and the paste both need. The settings page carries that state rather than going quiet. **I could not test the hotkey or the paste end to end** — both need a real desktop and a permission a script cannot grant itself, so that is the first thing to try when you run it.

- `src/shared/events.ts` — type-only `import type { TicketEvent } from './tickets'`, added as one arm of the union.

- `src/runner/index.ts` — threads `msg.tickets === true` into `runPrompt(..., tickets = false)` and adds `tickets ? ticketPreamble(this.httpBase, promptId) : ''` to the preamble list.

**Signatures**
```ts
ticketPut(promptId: string, raw: unknown): { ids: string[] } | { error: string }
ticketMove(promptId: string, ticketId: string, rawColumn: unknown, rawNote: unknown): Done
ticketDecide(promptId: string, ticketId: string, rawText: unknown): Done
ticketAsk(promptId: string, raw: Record<string, unknown>): Done
private ticketsOn(threadId: string): TicketAdded[]   // reads eventsOf(threadId), so a ghost reads its own transcript
type Done = { ok: true } | { error: string }
```

**Where it went differently**
- There is no `CrewEvent`. The union is `SessionEvent`, so `TicketEvent` went in there.
- `session.ts` already owns a module-level `TITLE_LIMIT = 80` for thread titles, so tickets' one is imported as `TITLE_LIMIT as TICKET_TITLE_LIMIT`.
- Move and decide return `{ok:true} | {error}` rather than a bare boolean, so each refusal is its own sentence the way `subagentSpawn`'s are. Statuses are as specified: 400 on put and question, 404 on move and decide.
- `game.score` and `music.added` are trimmed in `events.ts`'s `EPHEMERAL_KINDS`, and that list is shared with the renderer's own `trimEvents`. Adding ticket kinds there would also strip them from the renderer's live store, which is exactly where the other agent's `useTicketEvents` reads from. So the trim is a `chatEvents()` helper in `session.ts`, applied to the snapshot and to the history page, since `olderEvents` feeds both and both are the chat being scrolled.
- Worth knowing: with the snapshot filtered, a window that reloads mid-thread has no ticket events until new ones land, so a board does not survive a reload unless something carries it in the snapshot. That is what the trim asks for, but the renderer side may want to hear it.
- The decision route matches an empty id (`/tickets//decision`) because `ticketDecide` allows one and hangs it off whatever is on doing.

Only two pre-existing test failures left to deal with, but Switchboard caught something critical: removing ticket events from the snapshot breaks the whole feature. A client reconnecting later won't see the board at all until fresh events arrive, which defeats the purpose of having snapshots in the first place.

The issue is that I conflated what the chat renders with what gets handed to connecting clients. Looking at how music tracks and game scores handle this—they're trimmed from the event list but preserved as separate snapshot fields like `tracks` and `scores`—I should do the same for tickets. Either I add a `tickets` field to the snapshot and have the renderer merge them back, or I skip trimming entirely and just have the chat fold ignore ticket event kinds.

Since ticket events are the actual record that `boardOf` folds, the simpler fix is to leave them in the snapshot's event list and make sure the chat fold ignores unknown kinds. The chat fold already switches on known kinds, so unknown ones get skipped anyway. This restores the "replays for free" property without the snapshot bloat concern—a board is only ~30 events, negligible compared to agent steps. step.text:
The issue is that `chatEvents` filters out ticket events from the snapshot, leaving a reconnecting window without the board state. I need to decide between two approaches: either stop filtering and let the chat fold handle unknown event types, or store ticket events as a separate snapshot field like the existing `todos` and `tools` fields. Let me check what pattern the codebase already follows.

Looking at how other state survives reconnection, the established pattern is clear — anything that must persist rides as a first-class snapshot field. A board is folded from events by design for the "replays for free" property, so carrying the ticket events themselves in the snapshot as `tickets: TicketEvent[]` is the right move. It's consistent with how `todos` and `tools` work, and while it does grow over a session, that's bounded by the number of tickets and threads, which is acceptable. Option A is simpler but riskier since it leaves board events in the client's event array where they could get trimmed away. Going with option B — adding the ticket events field to the snapshot and keeping them in the renderer's store.

The store will seed its `tickets` slice from the snapshot on load, then append incoming ticket events to that same slice as they arrive on the wire. `useTicketEvents` reads only from that slice, avoiding the need to merge and dedupe across multiple sources. This mirrors exactly how `todos` works. Now I need to update the protocol definition, the session snapshot generation, and wire up the store changes. I'm reconsidering whether to merge snapshot events into the existing `events` slice or create a separate one—merging would be simpler but `trimEvents` might drop them, so I should stick with a dedicated slice and check how the store handles `todos` to follow the same pattern.

step.text:
I need to check the TabPill and Composer components, then trace through the styling chain to understand how `user-select` is being applied. The critical detail is that `body` has `user-select: none` set as a base rule, so I need to see if `#root` or any ancestor components override this with `select-text` or similar utilities. I'm realizing the key issue: `user-select: none` on body might be overridden by library CSS from tldraw, blocknote, or xterm that sets `user-select: text` globally. But more importantly, `user-select: none` only prevents *user* selection — programmatic selection via `selectAll()` or `getSelection()` still works regardless of the CSS rule. has `UserSelect() == EUserSelect::kNone` and it's a user gesture, it returns early. When `webContents.selectAll()` is called from the browser, it goes through the editing command path with `SetSelectionBy::kSystem` rather than `kUser`, which means it might bypass the `user-select: none` restriction that applies to user gestures. Writing code examples... The real issue is that importing the actual components pulls in the entire electron preload chain at module scope, which is too risky. So I'll copy the markup faithfully with all the real ancestor elements traced up to the root, but I need to be careful to preserve the exact DOM structure so I can actually identify which ancestor is re-enabling selection. My plan is to render both approaches — the copied markup with real ancestors and the actual components — to see which one reveals the culprit.

I should also grep through all the CSS files the app loads (styles.css, tldraw.css, blocknote CSS, xterm.css, etc.) to find any rules that might override the user-select restriction, since unlayered CSS beats layered CSS in the cascade and could be the real cause.

I'm planning to create a temporary candidates file and a probe script to render a collage of icon options, capture it as a PNG, then clean up afterward—but I need to keep the file accessible so Jamel can review the collage before I delete it.

Now I'm sketching out the actual icon designs with a 24-grid constraint, stroke weight of 2, rounded caps, and 2-3 marks per icon. The feature is a voice-to-text function, so I'm exploring different visual approaches: the current nib-on-a-rule design, and a new wave-into-a-rule concept where a zigzag path smooths into a straight line to suggest speech becoming written text. I'm working through the sizing constraints—the wave needs enough amplitude to read at 16 pixels, and I'm figuring out how the keyline dimensions work with a bare stroke run.

I'm also considering alternative approaches: three vertical bars of different heights standing on a baseline to represent both talking and writing (though it risks looking like an equalizer), a rounded page with a waveform inside it, a text cursor with a sound arc, and a pen stroke that's itself a wave. Each has tradeoffs in terms of clarity and visual impact at small sizes.

The strongest contender so far is treating the pill shape itself as the icon—a stadium with bars inside it, which feels very on-brand since the mark becomes the feature's visual identity. At 16 pixels, the outline and internal bars would need careful spacing to remain legible. The idea of text lines where the top one is a wave works well—it reads as a paragraph with a spoken first line, capturing both the "said and written" concept. I'm also considering a quote-like nib and a caret with a rule, plus thinking about what single distinctive mark defines each icon: the nib's vent hole or a wave's crest. Now I'm sketching out nine candidates on a 24-pixel grid, starting with the wave-to-rule concept as a continuous path. Simplifying the wave path with two humps followed by a straight section using quadratic curves for a cleaner, more legible result. Adjusting the control offset to -8 gives me a peak deviation of 4 and total height of 8, which feels better at the 16px scale. I'm reconsidering the path with three full humps plus a damped one—that's too much detail crammed into 12 units of width, making each hump only about 2.7 pixels wide. I think two humps max is the way to go. I'm considering whether the angular zigzag approach with round joins reads better than curves at small sizes—it's sharper but still soft enough to fit the brief. I'll sketch out both versions to compare. For a second candidate, I'm exploring a levels-based icon with stacked bars of varying heights on a baseline, though I need to figure out how many bars work best and whether that reads as a sound visualization rather than just a chart. A nib drawn at an angle with a wave trailing behind it could work, though I'd need to avoid duplicating the existing pencil glyph. I'm also considering a page with a wave inside it, but that feels too similar to the existing document glyphs. The stadium shape with three bars inside is more distinct, as is the idea of three text lines where the top one becomes a wave, with rules positioned at specific heights to create rhythm.

At size 16, that wave-and-lines approach reads clearly as three horizontal marks and could suggest "spoken text written down" or "transcript." It wouldn't collide with the framed document or checklist glyphs since this has no frame—just the lines themselves. I'm also exploring a bold quotation mark sitting on a rule to convey "what you said, written down," which would be visually strong at 16.

The wave-in-a-rounded-square idea is interesting too—a key cap with a wave inside it, suggesting "hold this key and talk"—though it risks reading as a button or keyboard key. So I'm narrowing down to the strongest candidates: the curved wave-to-rule, the angular version, levels on a rule, centered levels alone, the nib with rule, the nib with wave trail, the transcript style with wave and text rules, and the stadium pill with levels inside.

I'll render each one carefully at multiple sizes—48, 24, 20, and 16—on cards to see how they hold up, plus mock them in a toolbox tile and settings rail so I can judge them in context. Now I need to establish the baseline measurements and start drawing these out with proper coordinates.

For the stroke width, a bare line should sit at 15 units wide, but I'm realizing some of these marks might be wider runs at 18, which could flag the audit. Still, I should respect the constraint—a wave-to-rule mark is essentially a bare run, so it needs to reach from 4.5 to 19.5 to hit that 15-unit width. The diagonal extent gets trickier though; a 15-wide, 8-tall wave would reach about 17 units diagonally. I need to check the icon-geometry module to understand exactly how the family and size measurements work so I can draw to spec.

step.text:
I'm noticing a path resolution issue where Vite is using the process's current working directory instead of the specified root directory. On macOS, `/tmp` is a symlink to `/private/tmp`, so when I set `root: '/tmp/selp'`, it normalizes to that path, but Vite resolves the HTML file to `/private/tmp/selp/index.html` instead, suggesting it's falling back to the repo's working directory for resolution.

The fix is to resolve the temporary directory to its real path using `fs.realpath` after creating it with `mkdtemp`, since `tmpdir()` itself returns a symlinked path on macOS that needs to be normalized.

You were right, and the empty board is the proof.

**Why it was blank.** The columns were read off the task list each CLI keeps for itself. Claude Code has since dropped `TodoWrite` for `TaskCreate` and `TaskUpdate`, which never carry a list: the two rows in your screenshot are the whole payload, `{"taskId":"1","status":"completed"}`. Nothing to fold, so nothing on the board. The questions and decisions half was blank for a plainer reason: that thread was not opened with `/tickets`, so no brief ever reached me. One vendor renamed one tool and the feature was gone inside a day.

**So the harness is Crew's now.** `/tickets` is four calls on the host's own http, exactly the way `/agents/spawn` already works: put the work up and get an id for each, move one, name a decision, raise a question. It is a curl line in the preamble, so every provider gets the same board at once and none of it depends on what any CLI happens to expose. Every call names the promptId of the run asking, which is the same credential helpers use, so a board is reachable from its own thread and nowhere else.

Each call is written down as one event on the thread and `boardOf` folds the whole board back out of them, so it replays for free and is the same on everyone's screen. The CLI's own list is still read, demoted to a fallback: a thread that never puts a ticket up still gets rough columns for nothing, and the moment the agent keeps its own board those win outright.

Two things turned up that were breaking it underneath. `handleStep` on the host was dropping `todos` when it merged a step, so even the fallback never reached anybody. And filtering ticket events out of the snapshot, which I had asked for, meant a board would empty on every reload, so they ride in the snapshot as their own list the way the shelf and the todos do.

I sent two helpers out, one on the runner fallback and one on the host wiring, and took the shared core, the panel and the docs myself.

`yarn tsc --noEmit` is clean apart from two pre-existing errors in `tests/window-chrome.test.ts` that are somebody else's in-flight work. 31 tests across `tickets`, `ticket-api` and `step-todos` pass, and the session, ghost, subagent, provider and thread suites still pass.

One thing to know before you look: this is host and runner code, so it needs the app restarted rather than reloaded. Until then the window will keep running the old server.

Now I'm working through the visual design with specific measurements—grid at 24, center at 12, the live range from 2.25 to 21.75, and a stroke width of 2. I'm starting with the first candidate, a WaveRule that shows a spoken line transitioning into written form, using a single continuous path with two humps on the left side that flatten out on the right, constructed with quadratic curves for smooth damping.

I'm calculating the arc length and checking whether this shape qualifies as a "line" by measuring its reach against the keyline threshold—the horizontal span is 17.5 units but the keyline is 15, putting it 17% over budget. Since the enclosed area is small and the gap is open, it does classify as a line, but it's flagged as oversized. I'm adjusting the design to fit within the 15-unit reach by compressing the width and redistributing the hump amplitudes, starting fresh with a tighter configuration. Sketching out the wave as a series of chevron-like peaks and valleys, then flattening to a horizontal line at the end. The path reaches from 4.5 to 19.5, giving me the width of 15 I'm aiming for.

Now moving on to the "Levels" icon — three vertical bars of varying heights standing on a baseline rule. The bars are positioned at x = 7.5, 12, and 16.5, stretching from y = 6 down to y = 17, with the baseline sitting at y = 20.5 across the full width. Four bars centered without a rule to create a pure voice mark, positioned at x = 5.25, 9.75, 14.25, 18.75. I'm trying asymmetric heights like 5, 12, 8, 15 to avoid an equalizer look, but considering five bars instead for a more natural waveform appearance. Writing the nib SVG path... Adjusting the wave path to fit within the nib width, trying different hump configurations to center it properly between x 4.5 and 19.5. Finishing the wave path with two horizontal rules below it to represent text lines — the box spans 15 units wide and 16 tall, which reads clearly as audio transcribed into written form. I'm a bit concerned it might look like a wifi signal over text, but the wave-over-lines combination should read distinctly as speech-to-text rather than just a document with a squiggle.

Now moving on to the pill icon concept, which would use the Scribe pill shape itself with internal levels to show the layering.

For the pill proportions, I'm testing a 19×9 stadium shape since the app's pill is much wider than it is tall. The math shows that's about 23% under the target size, which is flagged as slightly small. The internal bars would be tight at that scale — roughly 3.3 pixels with 1.33 pixel strokes at 16px — but I'll sketch it as a candidate anyway, though I suspect it won't be the strongest option.

A better direction might be swapping those bars for a wave pattern instead, which could read more naturally as "hold the key." For the keycap option, I'm considering a 17×17 rounded square with a wave flowing through it — the wave itself would be quite delicate at that size, maybe 6.7 pixels wide and 3.3 pixels tall, which is risky but could work visually. And for the quote mark concept, I'm thinking of solid quotation marks positioned above a horizontal rule to suggest "what was said or written."

Actually, that reads too much like a blockquote, and DocGlyphs already has a quote mark, so I'm pivoting to a text caret with sound arcs instead — an I-beam cursor flanked by two curved lines to suggest dictation happening right where you're typing. I'm sketching out a vertical caret bar with arcs on either side, which would be just three marks total and conveys the idea of a cursor speaking.

Now I'm settling on my final nine glyphs: WaveRule and WaveRuleAngular for speech becoming text, LevelsRule and Levels for audio bars, Nib for the pen, NibWave for pen over handwriting, Transcript for wave over text rules, KeyWave for a keycap with a wave, and Caret for the cursor with sound arcs.

I'm reconsidering whether the WaveRule shape—a wave flattening into a line—will read clearly at 16 pixels, but I think it works fine as a visual metaphor for sound becoming text. Time to write out the SVG paths with precise coordinates.

Writing SVG paths... The path tokenizer correctly interprets the repeated coordinate pairs as implicit line commands, so the points trace through (4.5,12), (7,7.5), (9.5,16.5), (12,9.5), (13.5,12), and then horizontally to (19.5,12). The bounding box stays centered at (12,12) with the y-range 7.5–16.5, and the short peak between the last two points creates a nice damped effect. Now I'm moving to the levels rule, which uses vertical bar segments at different heights. Finishing the bar coordinates and checking the centering for the levels section. I'm positioning four bars at x 6, 10, 14, 18 to get the horizontal center right at 12, then setting their heights so they span from y 5 to 19 with the visual center landing at 12.

Now moving into the nib and wave elements — I'm taking the original nib path and adjusting its vertical range from 2.75 to 15.5.

+ ---
+ name: crew-copy
+ description: Write or fix the words in Crew. Use whenever a label, a line under a label, a button, an empty state, a placeholder, a toast, a menu row or a settings page is being written or reworked. Holds the test a line has to pass, the things never to say, and where each rule came from.
+ ---
+ 
+ # Writing the words in Crew
+ 
+ The Writing section of `AGENTS.md` is the law. Everything below is either that
+ section restated with its reasoning shown, or guidance from outside that agrees
+ with it. Where an outside source and `AGENTS.md` disagree, `AGENTS.md` wins and
+ the outside source is wrong for this project.
+ 
+ The failure this skill exists to stop is copy that reads as though a machine
+ wrote it: a line under every heading whether or not there was anything to say, a
+ sentence that hands back the brief it was built from, and an explanation of why
+ the software is the way it is.
+ 
+ ## The test
+ 
+ Every line has to pass all four. A line that fails any of them comes out.
+ 
+ 1. **Does it say something the screen cannot say on its own?** If the label, the
+    control, the icon or the surrounding page already says it, the line is a row
+    of type spent on nothing. Polaris: "Only add content that's necessary for
+    clarity" and "Let visuals and icons do the talking wherever you can."
+ 2. **Is it about the person, or about the machine?** Yifrah's basic rule is
+    "Don't talk about yourself or your product; talk about them." A line that
+    names a platform, a model, a permission mechanism, a file, a process or a
+    reason the code is shaped the way it is has failed.
+ 3. **Would it survive being read out loud?** Polaris: "Read it out loud. Does it
+    sound like something a human would say?" Mailchimp: "it's always more
+    important to be clear than entertaining."
+ 4. **Is every word in it earning its place?** GOV.UK: "put the important words
+    first and drop any unnecessary words." NN/g measured it: concise copy tested
+    58% more usable than the promotional baseline, objective copy 27% more, and
+    all three treatments together 124% more.
+ 
+ ## Never explain the machinery
+ 
+ This is the one that gets broken most, and it is the reason most Crew copy reads
+ as LLM output. A line that explains why something works the way it does is a
+ line written from the conversation that built the feature, not from what the
+ person is looking at.
+ 
+ GOV.UK states it as a design rule rather than a writing one: "If you find
+ yourself having to explain how the user interface works, that's a sign something
+ has gone wrong. Fix the interface." NN/g say the same about tooltips, which are
+ "highly contextual and specific and don't explain the bigger picture or entire
+ task flow", and about errors: "Avoid technical jargon and use language familiar
+ to your users instead."
+ 
+ Things that are machinery and never go in the app:
+ 
+ - **A platform limitation.** "macOS keeps Fn to itself, so no app is given it."
+   Nobody is owed a reason a key is not on a list. The list is the answer.
+ - **What is being downloaded, cached, compiled or spawned.** "A small model comes
+   down the first time." The person asked for dictation, not a build log.
+ - **Why a fallback exists.** "Use Control Command Space instead, which always
+   works." The "which always works" is the engineer saying the other one
+   sometimes does not, out loud, in the product.
+ - **How a rule is implemented.** "Marks and capitals, placed from how you said
+   it." The second half is the algorithm.
+ - **A named internal concept.** Not the panel, not the mode, not the mechanism,
+   not the model, not the hook, not the worker.
+ 
+ The line to write instead is the consequence for the person, or no line.
+ 
+ ## A heading stands on its own
+ 
+ A line under a heading that says the heading again in longer words is the
+ commonest bad line in a settings page, and it is invisible to whoever wrote it
+ because it reads as thorough. NN/g's microcontent rule is that a headline has to
+ "work out of context", and GOV.UK give the shape of the failure exactly:
+ "there's usually no need to say 'This is the total cost'. Just say 'Total cost'."
+ 
+ Two more shapes of the same mistake:
+ 
+ - **Naming back what the person is already looking at.** A line under a list of
+   keys that says these are the keys.
+ - **The flourish on the end.** "cursors and all", "and more", "in seconds",
+   "which always works". Filler taught in one screen is filler ignored in every
+   screen after it.
+ 
+ Start with nothing under the heading and add a line only when there is a fact
+ that has nowhere else to live. GOV.UK: "start with less. If you're creating a
+ form, start with some simple questions and only add help text if user research
+ shows that you need it." Polaris put it as a warning about components: "design
+ doesn't always dictate content (not every situation calls for subcopy, even if
+ the component has been designed to include it)." A `Row` in
+ `settings/parts.tsx` takes an optional `line` for exactly this reason. Leave it
+ off.
+ 
+ ## Labels, switches and rows
+ 
+ Apple's Human Interface Guidelines give the rule for a switch, and it is the
+ rule for every switch on every Crew settings page:
+ 
+ > If the setting label isn't enough, add an explanation. Describe what it does
+ > when turned on, and people can infer the opposite.
+ 
+ So a switch never gets two lines, one for on and one for off, and never gets a
+ line at all when its label already carries it. "Stutters" under a section called
+ "Tidying" is finished. "Fillers" is not, because nobody agrees on what one is,
+ so it gets three examples and no sentence: "Um, uh, you know."
+ 
+ The rest of the label rules:
+ 
+ - **Front-load.** GOV.UK's inverted pyramid: the most important point first, in
+   the page, the section, the paragraph and the sentence. Apple: put the most
+   important information first.
+ - **A button is a verb.** Apple: "when labeling buttons and links, it's almost
+   always best to use a verb." Polaris: "Start sentences with verbs so they feel
+   like actionable instructions."
+ - **Be direct.** Polaris: "Be direct ('add apps' not 'you can add apps')."
+ - **No politeness furniture.** GOV.UK: "There's usually no need to say 'please'
+   or 'please note'" and "There's usually no need to say thank you."
+ - **Labels live outside the field.** NN/g on placeholders: "the best solution is
+   to have clear, visible labels that are placed outside empty form fields", and
+   "Hints and instructions should also be persistent and placed outside of the
+   field." Where a placeholder is the only thing there is room for, as in a
+   two-column list, it has to read as a column heading and never as an
+   instruction or an example value.
+ 
+ ## When something has gone wrong
+ 
+ NN/g's error message guidelines are two halves and both are needed. The problem:
+ "Generic messages such as An error occurred lack context. Provide descriptions
+ of the exact problems." The way out: "Merely stating the problem is also not
+ enough; offer some potential remedies."
+ 
+ So a failure row is the state, plainly, and then the one thing to do about it.
+ It is never the reason. GOV.UK again: "do not say 'You have entered the wrong
+ password'. Say 'Wrong password'."
+ 
+ A toast is a moment and never a record, which is already in `AGENTS.md`. What
+ the sources add is why the temptation is wrong: NN/g found unsolicited help is
+ "often ignored by users because they get in the way: people want to use the
+ interface, not just read about it."
+ 
+ ## Voice
+ 
+ Dropbox's writing team, per John Saito, hold three words: simple, straightforward
+ and human. Podmajersky's four are purposeful, concise, conversational and clear.
+ Mailchimp: "We strip all that away and value clarity above all" and "we avoid
+ distractions like fluffy metaphors and cheap plays to emotion."
+ 
+ Crew's own, from `AGENTS.md`, are stricter and they win:
+ 
+ - **No em dashes, ever, and no semicolons standing in for one.** Plain sentences.
+ - **Crew is capitalized wherever it is named.** It is a name, not a word.
+ - **UI copy is for everyone.** No engineering jargon.
+ - **No emoji in the UI.** No branding beyond the word Crew.
+ - **A label like "You" goes in a `Pill`, never in parentheses.**
+ - **Copy never echoes the request that produced it.** If a line could be read
+   back as the feature request, rewrite it from what is on the screen.
+ 
+ Mailchimp's rule on jokes is the one to hold when a line starts feeling clever:
+ "don't go out of your way to make a joke, forced humor can be worse than none at
+ all." Crew has a voice and it is dry. It gets there by being exact, not by being
+ funny.
+ 
+ ## Write the words first
+ 
+ Jason Fried: "Since copywriting is interface design, you can do an awful lot of
+ great design in a text editor." And: "Don't worry about where things will go, or
+ how they will fit. Worry about explaining it clearly and then build the rest of
+ the interface around that explanation."
+ 
+ If a screen cannot be written plainly, the screen is wrong and no amount of copy
+ will cover it. That is the same finding as GOV.UK's "fix the interface", arrived
+ at from the other end.
+ 
+ Intercom's six questions are the fastest way to unstick a line that will not
+ come: who is it for, when do they see it, what do they need to know, what must
+ they do now, how is it delivered, and what tone does the app speak in.
+ 
+ ## Before and after
+ 
+ Real lines from this app.
+ 
+ | before | after | why |
+ | --- | --- | --- |
+ | "macOS keeps Fn to itself, so no app is given it." | nothing | A platform limitation. The list of keys is already the answer. |
+ | "A small model comes down the first time, and stays on this machine." | "Nothing you say leaves this machine." | The first half is machinery. The second half was the only fact worth a row of type, so it becomes the whole line. |
+ | "Use Control Command Space instead, which always works." | "Press Control Command Space instead." | Remedy kept, flourish cut. |
+ | "Crew needs it to see the key at all, and to put the words where you are typing." | "Dictation does nothing until it is on." | Two mechanisms became one consequence. The button beside it is the remedy. |
+ | "Marks and capitals, placed from how you said it." | nothing | The label is enough, and the rest was the algorithm. |
+ | "A word said twice on the way to the next one." | nothing | "Stutters" under "Tidying" says it. |
+ | "Um, uh, and a you know that is standing on its own." | "Um, uh, you know." | The examples were the useful part. "Standing on its own" was the rule's implementation. |
+ | "The first word lands whole, and your recording light is on the whole time." | "Your first word is never cut off, and your recording light stays on." | One benefit and one cost, both plain. A real trade said plainly is worth its row. |
+ | "The key is not being heard" | "Your key is not working" | Heard by what? Say it from where the person is standing. |
+ 
+ ## Checking it
+ 
+ There is no script for this. Read the screen top to bottom with every optional
+ line covered up, and put back only the ones whose absence you notice. Then read
+ what is left out loud.
+ 
+ Three questions that catch most of what survives that:
+ 
+ - **Cover the line. Is anything lost?** If not, it was never doing anything.
+ - **Could this sentence be pasted into the feature request it came from?** Then
+   it is the brief read aloud and it has to be rewritten from the screen.
+ - **Does it name a thing only somebody who built it would name?** A model, a
+   hook, a worker, a permission, a platform, a panel, a mode. Take it out.
+ 
+ ## Sources
+ 
+ - Nielsen Norman Group, [Concise, SCANNABLE, and Objective: How to Write for the Web](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/concise-scannable-and-objective-how-to-write-for-the-web/)
+ - Nielsen Norman Group, [Microcontent: How to Write Headlines, Page Titles, and Subject Lines](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/microcontent-how-to-write-headlines-page-titles-and-subject-lines/)
+ - Nielsen Norman Group, [Error-Message Guidelines](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/error-message-guidelines/)
+ - Nielsen Norman Group, [Help and Documentation (Usability Heuristic #10)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/help-and-documentation/)
+ - Nielsen Norman Group, [Tooltip Guidelines](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tooltip-guidelines/)
+ - Nielsen Norman Group, [Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/form-design-placeholders/)
+ - GOV.UK Service Manual, [Writing for user interfaces](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/writing-for-user-interfaces)
+ - GOV.UK, [Content principles: conventions and research background](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/govuk-content-principles-conventions-and-research-background/govuk-content-principles-conventions-and-research-background)
+ - Apple, [Human Interface Guidelines: Writing](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/writing)
+ - Shopify Polaris, [Product content](https://polaris-react.shopify.com/content/product-content)
+ - Mailchimp, [Content Style Guide: Voice and Tone](https://styleguide.mailchimp.com/voice-and-tone/)
+ - Jason Fried, [Since copywriting is interface design, you can do an awful lot of great design in a text editor](https://signalvnoise.com/posts/3467-since-copywriting-is-interface-design-you)
+ - Kinneret Yifrah, *Microcopy: The Complete Guide*
+ - Torrey Podmajersky, *Strategic Writing for UX* (O'Reilly)
+ - John Saito, [on UX writing at Dropbox](https://www.intercom.com/blog/podcasts/dropbox-john-saito-ux-writing/)
+ - Intercom, [Writing an interface](https://www.intercom.com/blog/videos/writing-an-interface/)
+

Looking at the icon candidates now. The current Nib design reads as a location pin at 64px because of the dot inside—that's definitely the issue Jamel flagged. NibWave has the same problem, even more pronounced. LevelRule works better conceptually with the bars sitting on a baseline, though at smaller sizes the rule gets too tight and the bars nearly merge with it, making it feel more like a generic bar chart. Levels is cut off but I'm evaluating how these scale.

Pill reads as a toggle switch, which isn't right. Transcript has potential with the wave over two rules, but the wave is too shallow and sits too close to the lines—they need more breathing room and the rules should be positioned lower and wider apart. The WaveAngle, WaveRule, and WaveStop variants are getting cut off at the bottom of the viewport, and they're reading as ECG or heartbeat lines, which isn't the direction I want. I need to expand the canvas height to see the full grid, and I'm realizing the alphabetical ordering is coming from how the exports are structured.

Before showing this to Jamel, I should refine the candidates—maybe replace Pill with something stronger and reconsider NibWave since the nib reads more like a pin. I'm thinking about alternatives like a wave inside a rounded text field (which directly shows the feature of dictation flowing into where you're typing), or a waveform that doubles as an underline beneath text. These feel more intentional than the current duds.

The wave family is the strongest direction overall. I want to tighten WaveRule by reducing the flat section and adding more humps so it reads better at smaller sizes, and WaveStop already works well with its dot. I'm also exploring a wave with a caret at the end to suggest the voice landing at your cursor position.

Let me lock in a final set of nine icons: WaveRule, WaveAngle, WaveStop, WaveCaret, LevelRule, Levels, an improved Transcript with a wave over written lines, Field with a wave inside a rounded rectangle, and Nib as a reference point.

Now I'm refining the geometry—dropping Pill and NibWave, then adjusting the Transcript icon so the wave sits deeper and the rule lines spread further apart. I'm testing different wave amplitudes to find the right balance where the peaks don't extend too far into the edge, settling on a configuration where the wave peaks sit at comfortable positions and the rules align cleanly below. At 16px the wave gets pretty tight with 3 humps, so I'll stick with that for the Transcript icon since it reads clearly as sound. For the Field component, I'm using a rounded rectangle paired with the wave, sizing the rect to give a geometric mean around 16.7 units.

Now I'm working on the WaveCaret icon, sketching out a similar wave pattern but with different control points to get the right amplitude and spacing.

For the LevelRule component, the bars are sitting too close to the rule line at 16px scale—there's only about 2.2 pixels of gap after accounting for stroke width. I'm pushing the rule down to y 20 and adjusting the bar bottoms to 15.5, which gives me closer to 1.7 pixels of breathing room. The bar tops stay at 9, 4.25, and 10.75.

The box now spans from y 4.25 to 20 with a center at 12.1, and with the stroke included, it fits within the live area at 21. I'm updating the candidates file and keeping the four-bar level configuration as is.
Now I can judge them. The nib reads as a map pin, the pill reads as a toggle. Reworking the set.

step.text:
The spine was working the whole time. It was the screen.

## What was wrong

Every event names the thread it happened on, and `ThreadView` gathers a thread's events with `e.threadId === threadId`. The two events a helper raises are the one pair that break that rule: `subagent.started` carries the *helper's* own thread id, and the thread it belongs to is `parentThreadId`. So the parent filtered its own chips out, and the helper's thread matched instead, where a chip would have pointed at itself.

The same filter was written out by hand in four places, so it was wrong in all four.

## The proof it was only the screen

Your log has every spawn you made, and they ran:

```
START Prover     | rendering the real chrome and selecting it
START Sweeper    | chrome sitting inside selectable content   END ok 4m 01s
START Glyph      | drawing the Scribe mark                    END ok 20m 23s
START Switchboard| wiring the board onto the host http         END ok 8m 51s
START Ledger     | reading the per-task tool shape             END ok 8m 43s
```

Nine helpers, all returned ok, answers folded back into their parents' turns. None of it ever had anywhere to land on screen.

## The fix

`eventsOfThread` in `components/thread.ts` is the rule, written once and used by all four views. A subagent event reads on `parentThreadId`, everything else reads on `threadId`.

`tests/subagent-chip-probe.test.ts` holds it: the chip lands in the thread that sent it and not in the helper, the end folds onto the chip that stands where it started, a breath of helpers folds into one row.

34 tests across 7 suites pass, `yarn tsc --noEmit` is clean for everything I touched, `yarn build` builds.

## What you'll see

This is renderer only, so it hot-reloads. No host restart this time.

The chips you already earned should appear retroactively in the threads that sent them, since the events are sitting in the log waiting. Under Bubbles' line you'll get a row: the generated mark, the subject, and either the latest step while it works or how long it took. Click one and the helper opens in the side panel as an ordinary thread with a composer that steers just that agent.

If the window doesn't pick it up, a reload will.

- // first thing to go: the flanks close in as they fall, so by the time a slit is
- // long enough to read it has under a pixel of counter either side and the whole
- // bottom of the mark fills in as one blob. The vent hole alone says nib and it
- // sits high, where the shape is still wide enough to hold it. And the line runs
- // wider than the nib rather than under it, because a bar the same width as the
- // shape above it is a plinth: what it has to read as is a rule on a page that

+ // The bars on the pill, which is the whole of what Scribe looks like while it is
+ // running. It is not a second microphone: that one is Voice and the two stand
+ // near each other in the toolbox, so this one is what a voice does rather than
+ // what it is spoken into.
+ //
+ // Four bars and not five. The mark is worn at 16, where five over the same width
+ // leaves under two pixels of gap and the run closes into a block. Every bar is
+ // centred on the same line, which is what tells a level meter from a chart: a
+ // set of bars standing on a floor is read as quantities beside each other, and
+ // one growing both ways off a middle is read as loudness. The tall one stands

While waiting for the Prover, I want to document a useful insight about the "paint vs copy" distinction — specifically that placeholders inside fields get painted but never copied, making them invisible to string-based selection tests, whereas pixel-reading tools like yarn selection-check can detect them.

I'll create a new memory entry called `crew-selection-paint-vs-copy` to capture this and update the memory index.

I need to capture pixel differences before and after selectAll for each element, using the bitmap data from the page capture. For the implementation, I'll grab the full bitmap from `capturePage()`, derive the device pixel dimensions from the bitmap length and the DIP size, then iterate through each piece's rect to count pixels where any channel differs by more than 8. I'll also capture the placeholder using the textarea's full rect since the text sits at the top. Running this for both A and B first, then C if time allows.

+ ---
+ name: crew-selection-paint-vs-copy
+ description: "What a selection paints and what it copies are different answers, so selection bugs need yarn selection-check and not a source or clipboard test"
+ metadata:
+   node_type: memory
+   type: feedback
+ ---
+ 
+ In Crew the renderer defaults to `user-select: none` on the body and content asks
+ for it back with `select-text`. Two things that rule cannot be tested for by
+ reading the stylesheet or by reading `getSelection().toString()`:
+ 
+ - A **placeholder** sits inside a field, and fields are `user-select: text`, so a
+   select all painted a highlight over every placeholder in the app while
+   **never** putting it in the selection string. Paint and copy are two different
+   answers. The fix is `input:placeholder-shown, textarea:placeholder-shown {
+   user-select: none }` in the base layer.
+ - Chromium honors `user-select: none` for drags, `execCommand('selectAll')` and
+   `webContents.selectAll()` alike, so chrome that looks selectable in a running
+   window is usually a **window running an older renderer**, not a broken rule.
+ 
+ **Why:** a suite that reads `styles.css` and a probe that reads the clipboard
+ both passed the whole time every field was highlighting its own words.
+ 
+ **How to apply:** `yarn selection-check` (`scripts/selection-check.mjs`) builds
+ the real stylesheet with the Tailwind `@source` trick, selects everything in a
+ real Electron window, and diffs the bitmaps before and after per element box. Run
+ it for anything touching selection. `webContents.selectAll()` does nothing on a
+ window with `show: false`. Related: [[crew-look-at-renderer-ui]].

I found the issue — `getSize()` is already returning device pixels (2580x1144), so the scale factor is 1, which is correct. The selection is being painted across 40495 pixels in the frame, but the per-box counts were zero because I was comparing CSS pixel coordinates from `getBoundingClientRect()` against device pixel coordinates, sampling from the wrong location entirely.

The fix is to compute the actual scale factor properly by dividing the device width by the CSS viewport width — I'll grab `devicePixelRatio` and `innerWidth` from the page to calculate this correctly (2580 / 1290 = 2), then apply that scale when sampling the boxes.
